ann_35.text: This part acts on 107 of 242 training patients (44%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 85% without this part to about 90% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 70 of these 107 patients had heart disease.

Through this part, maximum heart rate only lowers the predicted risk of heart disease while it stays below about 167 beats per minute (between 151 and 167 beats per minute for different patients): for a typical such patient, going from 111 beats per minute to 202 beats per minute moves it from about 68% to about 45% (on the training data only).

Through this part, the model treats a higher maximum heart rate as lowering the predicted risk of heart disease steadily up to about 167 beats per minute (between 151 and 167 beats per minute for different patients), then no further: for a typical patient, it goes from about 68% at 118 beats per minute to about 48% at 175 beats per minute (on the training data only).

ann_36.text: This part acts on 2 of 242 training patients (1%); nearly all of them are patients with thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded).

For a typical patient it acts on, it raises the predicted risk of heart disease from below 1% without this part to about 9% with it (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 2 training patients (patients the part acts on).
In the training data, 1 of these 2 patients had heart disease.

Through this part, for a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded) applies (about 99%) than if thallium stress test result is something other than thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded) (about 54%) (on the training data only). ann_38.text: This part acts on 141 of 242 training patients (58%); nearly all of them are patients without chest pain on exercise.

summary.text: For a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 1%) than if the patient is a man (about 54%) (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 9%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 54%) (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: for a typical patient, it goes from about 54% at 0 vessels to about 97% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

The model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 54% to about 1% if exercise does not bring on chest pain, and from about 16% to about 16% if exercise brings on chest pain.

For a typical patient, going from chest pain type other than atypical angina to atypical angina moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 16% to about 1% if exercise brings on chest pain, and from about 54% to about 8% if exercise does not bring on chest pain.
The model ignores resting ECG and resting blood pressure.
